subject: Critical Thinking
title: Overconfidence: The Most Dangerous Bias in Decisions
description: A 60-second lesson on Overconfidence: The Most Dangerous Bias in Decisions.

hook.text: Ask people to give 90% confidence intervals for questions. They're right about 50% of the time.

buildup.text: Overconfidence: our confidence in our knowledge and predictions consistently exceeds our actual accuracy.

discovery.text: It appears in three forms: over-estimation, over-placement, over-precision.

twist.text: CEOs, doctors, lawyers, & investors are all chronically overconfident.

climax.text: Calibration training helps: practice giving probabilities & checking them.

punchline.text: You're probably wrong more often than you think. Literally.

quiz.question: What is calibration in the context of decision-making?
options: Matching confidence levels to actual accuracy rates

details.summary: Overconfidence is the tendency to believe your knowledge is more accurate and your predictions more reliable than they actually are. Studies show that when people say they are 90% confident, they are right only about 70% of the time.
details.whyItMatters: Overconfidence leads to under-preparation, excessive risk-taking, and the inability to learn from mistakes because you never expected to be wrong.
takeaways: People consistently overestimate the accuracy of their judgments
90% confidence intervals capture the true value only about 50% of the time
Calibration training can measurably reduce overconfidence

faq.question: How is overconfidence measured in research studies?
faq.answer: Researchers ask people to provide confidence intervals for factual questions. If 90% intervals should contain the true answer 90% of the time but only do 50%, the overconfidence gap is 40 percentage points.

faq.question: What practical steps can reduce overconfidence in everyday decisions?
faq.answer: Keep a prediction journal, widen your confidence intervals, actively consider reasons you might be wrong, and seek feedback from people who disagree. Tracking your actual accuracy is the fastest path to better calibration.
